    AI Overview
    humiliation
    Humiliation is
    a profoundly painful experience, often felt as intense social rejection or embarrassment, involving a loss of self-esteem and dignity caused by others. It is a powerful, often unjust exercise of power that induces shame. Overcome it by fostering self-compassion, using mindful breathing, maintaining positive posture, and shifting away from threat-based thinking. 
    Understanding Humiliation 
    • Core Aspects: It involves a severe, often public, loss of face or reputation.
    • The Experience: It is felt as deep humiliation, disgrace, or "mortification," often causing a feeling of being exposed or powerless.
    • Physical Reaction:
      Researchers have found that humiliation activates the same regions of the brain as physical pain.
    • Power Dynamic: It is often an act done by one party (person or institution) against another to exert power, often arbitrarily. 
    Role in Social Interactions 
    • Violation of Social Bonding: Unlike shame, which can be adaptive, humiliation serves no positive, adaptive function.
    • Weaponization: It is frequently used in social, professional, or political contexts to create a "winner" and a "loser".
    • Forms: Examples include public shaming, betrayal, exclusion, or violation of rights. 
    Coping and Overcoming Humiliation 
    • Self-Compassion: Cultivating a compassionate, understanding attitude toward oneself can help diminish the intense pain of humiliation.
    • Vagus Nerve Stimulation: Body-based practices like slowing one’s breath and calming one's physical reactions to stress can activate the parasympathetic nervous system.
    • Mindfulness: Practicing mindful awareness and having calm self-talk can shift one’s mindset from a threat-based state to a secure one.
    • Constructing a Stronger Self-Identity: Working on creating a "compassionate self-identity" that is strong, wise, and courageous can help protect against future experiences of humiliation. 
    Common Reactions 
    • Consequences: Individuals often suffer from low self-esteem, depression, social isolation, and, in severe cases, feelings of being "obliterated".
    • Shame vs. Humiliation: While shame involves feeling like you have done something wrong, humiliation is a feeling that you have been treated wrongly.

    Turn on your Visual Search History?

    Google uses its visual recognition technologies to process the images you use to search, like when you search with Google Lens. If you turn on your Visual Search History, Google will save these images from eligible Google services to your Web & App Activity when you’re signed in to your Google Account. You can learn more about this setting and which Google services save images to it at g.co/Search/VisualSearchHistory.

    How visual search history is used

    Your Visual Search History may be used to improve your experience on Google services, like letting you revisit your past visual searches. It may be used to develop and improve Google’s visual recognition and search technologies, as well as the Google services that use them.

    When visual search history is off

    If you turn this setting off, any previous Visual Search History may still be kept and used to improve Google’s visual recognition and search technologies, unless you delete it from your Web & App Activity.

    Visual Search History doesn’t affect images saved by other settings, like Gemini Apps Activity.

    How to manage your Visual Search History

    You can view, delete, or manage your Visual Search History at activity.google.com. To download your Visual Search History, visit takeout.google.com. Images will be deleted in accordance with your Web & App Activity auto-delete settings, although some types of images may be deleted sooner.

    Google uses and saves data in accordance with Google Privacy Policy.

    Coping Strategies. How can one cope with or overcome humiliation?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Coping with humiliation involves acknowledging the pain without judgment, practicing self-compassion, and separating your self-worth from the event. To move forward, take accountability if necessary, learn from the experience, and set boundaries to avoid future situations. Overcoming it requires time, resilience, and often, support from others. 
    Key Strategies for Coping and Overcoming:
    • Acknowledge and Own the Feeling:
      Don't let your mind twist the incident into something fictional; acknowledge what happened, but refuse to let it define you. Label the emotion without judging yourself, as suggested in a post on Rula. 
    • Put it in Perspective:
      Realize that most humiliating moments are temporary and not as personal as they feel. Most people are focused on their own lives and will forget the incident quickly. 
    • Use Humour or Vulnerability:
      If possible, laughing at yourself can disarm the humiliation and take the tension out of the situation. 
    • Learn and Adapt:
      Treat the event as a lesson, not a life sentence. Identify what you can do differently if a similar situation arises. 
    • Seek Support and Set Boundaries:
      Talk to trusted friends or a therapist to process the trauma and build resilience. Set firm boundaries with people who continue to make you feel uncomfortable. 
    • Practice Self-Compassion:
      Forgive yourself if the mistake was yours. Remember that mistakes are a part of being human. 
    If the humiliation is causing lasting trauma, therapy (like DBT or cognitive-behavioral techniques) can be helpful in addressing deep-seated shame.
